intro: You're crossing the river into the district Florence used for work, not for photographs. Behind Santa Croce's neo-Gothic facade there's a star nobody put there by accident, and in a square where fists once drew blood, a date is carved into a marble disc that almost nobody notices. You'll cross the Ponte Vecchio along the way, without stopping — that story already belongs to another route in this same city — to enter Oltrarno, the district where artisans have spent eight hundred years working leather, wood and gold with the same hands, generation after generation. It's just under 2.5 km and eight stops: here, the difficulty lies in noticing the small things, not the monumental ones.
puntoPartida: Piazza Santa Croce, facing the facade of the Basilica di Santa Croce

paradas.titulo: The Star That Shouldn't Be There
paradas.llegada: Standing in Piazza Santa Croce, face the basilica's main facade: geometric panels of white, green and pink marble covering the whole surface, crowned by a large rose window. Look up to the triangular gable that tops the facade, just above the rose window.
paradas.enigma: This facade looks medieval, matching the rest of the Gothic church, but it's actually 19th-century: it was finished in 1863 by architect Niccolò Matas, who was Jewish, almost 600 years after construction of the basilica began. Right at the centre of the triangular gable, amid the geometric marble decoration, Matas included a figure nobody would expect to find on the front of a Franciscan church: a star formed by two overlapping triangles, one inverted over the other. How many points does that star have?
pistas: Look right at the top point of the triangle crowning the facade, above the central rose window, not at the sides.
It's the same figure of two crossed triangles that appears on the flag of Israel.
It has 6 points: it's a hexagram, the Star of David.
paradas.historia: Matas died in 1872, without ever seeing the whole facade he'd spent half his life completing fully finished. Because he was Jewish, he couldn't be buried inside the basilica alongside the great names of Italy who rest there; he was buried right beneath the threshold of the main door, in the outer pavement, under a stone that thousands of visitors now walk over every day without knowing it. Some historians today point out that the hexagram was also a common decorative motif in 19th-century neo-Gothic architecture, not necessarily a personal signature — but the coincidence, up there, still doesn't go unnoticed by anyone who looks closely.
paradas.fuente: Wikipedia — Niccolò Matas, Basilica di Santa Croce; FirenzeToday — Perché sulla facciata di Santa Croce c'è la stella ebraica

paradas.titulo: The Disc That Marked the Centre of the Pitch
paradas.llegada: Without leaving Piazza Santa Croce, turn towards the long side of the square, on your left if the basilica is behind you: look for Palazzo dell'Antella, recognisable as the longest facade on the whole square, covered in traces of fresco painting. At ground-floor height, set into the stone, there's a small round white marble disc.
paradas.enigma: Since the Renaissance, this square has been the pitch for Calcio Storico Fiorentino: a violent sport, half football and half wrestling, pitting Florence's four historic districts against each other. In 1565, two marble discs were set into facades on opposite sides of the square — this one on Palazzo dell'Antella, and another on the building facing it — to permanently mark the line dividing the pitch exactly in half. The disc in front of you has a year carved into it: the very year the pitch was marked out. What year is it?
pistas: It's not the year of a famous match: it's the year the marble discs themselves were installed.
It's a year from the mid-16th century, when Florence was already ruled by the Medici as grand dukes.
The year carved is 1565.
paradas.historia: The most famous match ever played on this square took place on 17 February 1530, during the siege of Florence by the troops of Charles V: the besieged, starving city held its Carnival match anyway, as a gesture of defiance towards the enemy, even climbing onto nearby rooftops to play music so the imperial soldiers would hear it from outside the walls. Today, every June, a tournament between the four historic districts is still played here — Santa Croce (blue), Santa Maria Novella (red), San Giovanni (green) and Santo Spirito (white) — on a thick layer of sand covering the whole square during tournament weeks.
paradas.fuente: Comune di Firenze — Partita dell'Assedio; Wikipedia — Calcio storico fiorentino, Palazzo dell'Antella

paradas.titulo: The Three Arts Watching Over the Sculptor
paradas.llegada: Enter the Basilica di Santa Croce through the main door — there's an admission fee, around €8-11 depending on the ticket, which also covers the Museum, the Cloisters and the Pazzi Chapel; if you're not going in, read the story anyway and move on to stop 4. Once inside, look in the right-hand aisle, very close to the entrance, for a large marble funerary monument with three seated figures.
paradas.enigma: This basilica is known as the Temple of Italian Glories because Michelangelo, Galileo, Machiavelli and the composer Rossini, among others, are buried here. The tomb in front of you is Michelangelo's: it was designed by Giorgio Vasari, commissioned by Grand Duke Cosimo I, who had the artist's body brought from Rome in 1564. At the foot of the sarcophagus, several marble statues — each by a different sculptor — represent, one each, a different art in which Michelangelo was a master. How many allegorical statues are seated on this tomb?
pistas: It's not a single figure mourning the dead: there are several distinct statues, each representing an artistic discipline.
The three arts represented are Sculpture, Painting and Architecture.
There are 3 statues, one for each art.
paradas.historia: The monument wasn't finished until 1576, twelve years after Michelangelo's death, and each statue was carved by a different artist: Sculpture is by Valerio Cioli, Painting by Giovan Battista Lorenzi, and Architecture by Giovanni dell'Opera. Directly opposite, on the other side of the aisle, is the tomb of Galileo Galilei, moved here in 1737 — almost a century after his death — because the Church, which had condemned him in life, took generations to allow him a dignified burial inside a Christian church.
paradas.fuente: Opera di Santa Croce — Monumento funebre di Michelangelo (Vasari); Wikipedia — Basilica di Santa Croce

paradas.titulo: The Portrait That Arrived Three Centuries Late
paradas.llegada: Leave the square via Via Ghibellina, heading north-east, and walk about 400 m to number 70, on the corner with Via Buonarroti. This is Casa Buonarroti: houses that belonged to Michelangelo's family, now a museum. Without needing to go in, look at the facade, right above the main door.
paradas.enigma: Michelangelo bought these houses in 1508 and lived in them on and off, but the building you see today, in its current form, wasn't built by him: it was the work of his great-nephew, Michelangelo Buonarroti the Younger, between 1612 and 1643, who turned it into a monument to the artist's memory. Above the main door there's a bust representing Michelangelo himself, but it's not a portrait from his own lifetime: it was placed there in 1875, the work of Clemente Papi and Lodovico Caselli after a design by Daniele da Volterra, a friend of the artist. Michelangelo died in 1564. Counting in whole centuries, how many centuries passed between his death and this bust being placed above the door?
pistas: Subtract the year Michelangelo died (1564) from the year the bust was placed (1875).
The result is 311 years: rounded to whole centuries, that's several centuries, not just one or two.
3 centuries (311 years) passed between his death and the bust above the door.
paradas.historia: On the facade, next to the door, there's also a Buonarroti coat of arms in brightly coloured glazed terracotta, made in the early 1500s by the della Robbia family workshop — the same family who invented the blue-and-white ceramic technique seen all over Florence — much older than the bust. Inside, though this route doesn't go in, the world's largest collection of Michelangelo's original drawings is kept: over 200 sheets the family preserved across generations.
paradas.fuente: Casa Buonarroti — Storia del museo; Wikipedia — Casa Buonarroti

paradas.titulo: The Tower That Refused to Move
paradas.llegada: Head back towards the Arno — via Via de' Benci or Borgo Santa Croce, about 10 minutes — and cross the Ponte Vecchio without stopping: its goldsmiths' shops and their history already belong to another route in this same city. When you reach the south end of the bridge, right where you enter the Oltrarno district, stop on Via de' Bardi: look for a small medieval stone tower, almost touching the last houses of the bridge, older and rougher than everything around it.
paradas.enigma: This is the Torre dei Mannelli, from the 13th century: the only survivor of the four towers that once guarded the corners of the Ponte Vecchio. In 1565, when Giorgio Vasari built the elevated passageway that let the Medici cross from one palace to another without setting foot on the street, every other owner gave up part of their facade to let it run in a straight line... except the family who owned this tower, who flatly refused. Vasari had to divert the passageway, pushing it outward on projecting stone brackets to go around the tower without touching it: look up and find the stretch that breaks from the straight line. Which family refused to hand over their tower to the Medici?
pistas: The answer is in the very name the tower is known by.
It's a Florentine surname, the same one that names the tower: Torre dei ______.
It was the Mannelli family.
paradas.historia: The result of that standoff can still be seen today: the Corridoio Vasariano, almost a kilometre of elevated passageway, suddenly breaks from its straight line right at this point, held up by stone corbels that make it go around the tower on the outside before continuing on towards the Palazzo Pitti. It's the only stretch of the entire corridor that doesn't run straight — the exception one single surname managed to force onto the Medici.
paradas.fuente: Wikipedia — Torre dei Mannelli, Corridoio vasariano

paradas.titulo: The Door That Became a Window
paradas.llegada: Continue along Via de' Guicciardini for about 5 minutes to Piazza de' Pitti. Before you opens the stone facade of the Palazzo Pitti: an almost unbroken wall of enormous ashlar blocks, barely decorated, filling the entire width of the square. Look at the central block, taller than the wings on either side of it: it's the oldest part of the building.
paradas.enigma: When Luca Pitti commissioned this palace around 1458 — to a design attributed to Filippo Brunelleschi — the ground floor of the central block opened with three great stone doorways: one in the centre and one on each side. A century later, when the Medici bought the palace and had Bartolomeo Ammannati enlarge it, the two side doorways were closed off and turned into kneeling windows — taller than they are wide, resting on a scrolled stone ledge — leaving only one still in use. Look closely at the ground floor of the central block: of those three original doorways, how many are still real doors today, ones you could actually walk through?
pistas: The other two openings are still there, the same shape and size as a doorway, but you can no longer walk through them.
You can spot them by the scrolled stone ledge partway up, closing off the opening: these are the windows Ammannati called inginocchiate ('kneeling').
Only 1 real door remains today: the one in the centre.
paradas.historia: The palace you see today is far wider than the original: Eleonora di Toledo, Cosimo I's wife, bought it around 1550 as the family's new residence, and over the following centuries the Medici, and later the Lorraine, extended it with wings on both sides until it was several times its original width. Even so, the central block in front of you, its rustic ashlar blocks growing smaller with each storey, is still recognisable as the 15th-century core.
paradas.fuente: Wikipedia — Palazzo Pitti; FlorenceCity — La facciata barocca di Palazzo Pitti

paradas.llegada: Walk to Piazza Santo Spirito, about 5 minutes via Via Maggio and Sdrucciolo de' Pitti. Stand facing the Basilica di Santo Spirito and take in its entire facade, top to bottom.
paradas.enigma: Filippo Brunelleschi designed this church — one of the high points of the Florentine Renaissance, alongside the Duomo's dome — but he died in 1446, just two years after work began, without leaving a clear plan for the exterior facade. His pupils completed the interior following his designs, but they never built the monumental facade a building like this would be expected to have: today it's a plain whitewashed wall, flat, without a single column, statue, relief or rose window. Count how many decorative elements — statues, reliefs, mosaics — there are on this facade.
pistas: Don't look too hard for detail: it's a completely flat wall, whitewashed in plain white, with almost no relief at all.
Compare it mentally with the Santa Croce facade you visited at the start of the route, covered in marble and a carved star: there's nothing equivalent here.
There isn't a single decorative element: it's 0.
paradas.historia: The current smooth white plaster on the facade dates from the late 18th century, but the lack of decoration goes back to the very beginning. Inside, by contrast, Santo Spirito is extraordinarily rich, with dozens of side chapels and works by Filippino Lippi, among others. That contrast between a plain exterior and a lavish interior repeats itself in several Florentine churches of the period — starting with the Medici's own San Lorenzo, whose bare brick facade is still unfaced almost 500 years later — as if Florence had decided to save its money for what really mattered: the inside.

paradas.titulo: The Hands That Are Still Working
paradas.llegada: Finish by strolling down any of the artisan streets around this square — Via di Santo Spirito, Via Maggio, or a little further on, Borgo San Frediano: pick whichever you like, they're all full of workshops with their doors flung wide open. Look for a shop window or workshop door displaying a small official plaque or seal.
paradas.enigma: Oltrarno has been Florence's artisan district since the Middle Ages: tanners, woodcarvers, gilders and goldsmiths worked here for the palaces on the other bank, and many of those trades are still practised today, in the very same premises, sometimes by the same family for generations. The Comune di Firenze keeps an official register of historic and traditional activities that recognises and protects these workshops, requiring a minimum number of years of uninterrupted activity on the same premises to qualify. How many years of minimum activity does the Comune di Firenze's regulation require for a workshop or shop to be recognised as historic?
pistas: It's not 25 and it's not 100: it's a figure in between, half a century.
It's roughly the same number of years as a full working lifetime.
It requires 50 years of uninterrupted activity.
paradas.historia: Today more than 400 businesses and workshops across Florence carry this official recognition, a good number of them concentrated right here in Oltrarno, where the guild tradition never quite broke. You've crossed the river following the trail of a single surname — Buonarroti — turned into a genius and a museum; you end the route surrounded by hundreds of anonymous surnames who, with their hands, keep making, every day, the Florence that never makes it onto the postcards.
paradas.fuente: Comune di Firenze — Regolamento delle botteghe storiche

final.titulo: You've Crossed to the Other Side of Florence
final.texto: A six-pointed star a Jewish architect hid on the facade of a Franciscan basilica. A marble disc from 1565 marking the exact centre of a violent Renaissance football pitch. Three statues watching over the greatest sculptor of them all. A bust that arrived three centuries late. A tower that a single surname kept even the Medici from touching. A door that became a window. A facade its own architect left bare. And an entire district that, eight hundred years on, still works with its hands. The Duomo and Piazza della Signoria are the Florence that poses for the photo; Santa Croce and Oltrarno are the one still at work.
